title: Ravana rides out
hook: the king finally comes himself; the inner enemies that grow back
carry: six inner enemies, and they grow back

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kumbhakarna wakes, the giant who saw his brother was wrong and fought for him anyway. Tamas.
screen: `TAMAS: SEEING WHAT'S RIGHT, SLEEPING THROUGH IT.`

segments.voice: For the whole war, Ravana has sent other people. Generals. Sons. His giant brother. One by one, they've fallen. Kumbhakarna is gone. Now even Indrajit, his great son, the master of illusion, has been killed by Lakshmana. There's nobody left to send. So the king of Lanka puts on his armor, climbs into his chariot, and rides out through the gates himself. Ten heads. Twenty arms. A bow in several hands at once. After all these weeks, the serial brings the two of them face to face: Rama on foot, Ravana in the chariot.
screen: `EVERYONE HE SENT HAS FALLEN.` → `THE GATES OPEN.` → `FACE TO FACE, AT LAST.`

segments.voice: It's easy to make Ravana a cartoon, and the Ramayana doesn't. In the tradition he's a great scholar, learned in the Vedas, and a fierce devotee of Shiva; a hymn to Shiva's dance, the Shiva Tandava Stotram, is traditionally said to be his. Tradition makes him a veena player too. He's brave, and a real king to his people. And he took another man's wife by force and wouldn't give her back when everyone he trusted begged him to. That's the tragedy: all that greatness, bent around one refusal. Even his name carries a story. In the tradition, he once tried to lift Shiva's mountain, Kailasa, and Shiva pressed it down with one toe, pinning him. Ravana roared so loudly the worlds shook, and Shiva, in the Uttara Kanda's telling, named him Ravana: the one who made the worlds cry out. Now the fight. Rama cuts off one of Ravana's heads with an arrow, and another grows back in its place. He cuts another. It grows back. Over and over. Hindu teaching has a name for what keeps growing back: the six inner enemies, the shadripu. Desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy. Some teachers read Ravana's ten heads as those enemies; lists differ. Ravana had learning, devotion and courage, and it wasn't enough, because one enemy, desire, sat on the throne. That's the teaching: knowing the scriptures doesn't save you if the enemies inside are running things. It's why, at Dussehra, when the huge ten-headed effigies burn, many families say those are what's really burning. So start small: pick one, and say its name.
screen: `SCHOLAR, DEVOTEE, MUSICIAN, KING.` · `THE ONE WHO MADE THE WORLDS CRY OUT.` · `CUT ONE HEAD. ANOTHER GROWS.` · `SHADRIPU: SIX ENEMIES INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Picture ten heads without fear, and give them faces you might recognize: the six enemies first, desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, then whatever else yours are. Pick the one that showed up most this week, look it in the face without fighting it, and say its name quietly, inside. When it grows back, and it will, you'll recognize it faster.
Ravana, the one who made the worlds cry out: the great, learned, ten-headed king, out of people to send, finally facing Rama himself.
Your line: six inner enemies, and they grow back. Naming one is the first arrow. That's day sixty-five in the books.

howItsDone: At Dussehra, many communities in north India burn huge effigies of the ten-headed Ravana, and some teachers use the ten heads to speak about the inner faults that keep returning; the Shiva Tandava Stotram, attributed to Ravana, is chanted by devotees of Shiva.

Ravana.meaning: Lanka's ten-headed king; 'the one who made the worlds cry out'

Shiva.meaning: a great Hindu god; Ravana was his fierce devotee

Shiva Tandava Stotram.meaning: a hymn to Shiva's dance, traditionally said to be Ravana's

Kailasa.meaning: Shiva's mountain, which Ravana tried to lift

shadripu.meaning: the six inner enemies: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy

Dussehra.meaning: the autumn festival of Rama's victory, when Ravana effigies burn

notes: Indrajit's death at Lakshmana's hands is mentioned in passing; the outline has no separate day for it.
The heads growing back: in Valmiki, Rama cuts Ravana's heads and they regrow (Yuddha Kanda, before Agastya's counsel); confirm.
The ten heads as inner faults (kama, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, matsarya, etc.) is a common devotional reading, not Valmiki's; stated as 'many teachers read'. Confirm.
The Shiva Tandava Stotram's attribution to Ravana is traditional; confirm the phrasing 'traditionally said to be his'.
Name: Uttara Kanda story of Kailasa; Dashagriva as his earlier name. Confirm.
